cansatProject.title: CanSat Project
cansatProject.intro_p1: The CanSat challenge is an educational initiative by the European Space Agency. It challenges students aged 14 to 19 from all over Europe to build a mini satellite the size of a soda can. This small satellite must integrate all the essential systems: power, sensors and communication, plus a parachute for a safe landing.
cansatProject.intro_p2: The main purpose of CanSat is to foster interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM disciplines). By challenging students to design, build and launch a mini satellite the size of a soda can, they are taught how real aerospace technology actually works.
cansatProject.intro_p3: My classmates and I formed a team for the 2024 edition called "Clan nK". Unfortunately, we couldn't finish the project due to several issues: a member who didn't want to work, our Erasmus trip which split up the team, how difficult it was to work remotely, and a lack of time. Even so, we learned a lot along the way.
cansatProject.elec_p1: For this project we used an Arduino Uno R3 with several sensors. We had to learn from scratch how this type of device works with Arduino boards and how to wire them up. The components we used were the following:
cansatProject.elec_c1_desc: This is the real-time telemetry system. It allows data to be sent wirelessly from the satellite to a laptop; the purpose was to send the location in real time so the components could be recovered afterwards.
cansatProject.elec_c2_desc: This sensor measures barometric pressure and air temperature. It is the key piece for collecting atmospheric data during the mission, which is the main goal of the challenge.
cansatProject.elec_c3_desc: Receives signals from satellites to obtain geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) and the satellite's real-time speed. With the help of the radio frequency sensor we can locate the satellite once it lands, as well as get precise flight trajectory data.
cansatProject.elec_c4_desc: This sensor is used to monitor the intensity of ultraviolet radiation during the satellite's descent.
cansatProject.elec_c5_desc: Since the satellite is in flight and can't be connected to a computer, this module is used to store all the data collected by the sensors during the mission on an SD card in CSV format. We used this instead of the radio frequency module because, with so many satellites deployed at once and the distance involved, there could be interference or data loss; we decided this option was more reliable.
cansatProject.diagram_p1: This diagram was made to get an idea of how to wire up all the electronics on the Arduino with all the components mentioned above.
cansatProject.diagram_p2: We then assembled the components on the actual Arduino. The wiring was a bit messy, but everything was functional.
cansatProject.prog_p1: On this project we learned basic C++ programming and how to use the Arduino IDE, both from scratch. Our code continuously listens to the GPS module, which gives us the exact position (latitude and longitude), date and time. At the same time, the pressure and temperature sensor tells us the temperature and the current atmospheric pressure, and from that pressure it calculates an estimate of our altitude. There is also an additional sensor that measures the ambient ultraviolet radiation.
cansatProject.prog_p2: All this data is organized and sent in a clear, structured format, with the identifier "CLAN NK" at the start of each line, which makes it easier to read or import into a spreadsheet later. The code also drives the radio frequency module, which sends all this data to the receiver — in our case, a laptop.
cansatProject.prog_p3: We didn't have time to implement the SD card part in the main code, but we did run a test using "hello world".
cansatProject.mod_p1: I took care of all the 3D modeling myself. For the CanSat we were given exact measurements to build the satellite's casing around — the same as a 330 ml soda can: 66 mm in diameter and 115 mm in height.
cansatProject.mod_p2: This made things quite complicated, since on top of that we wanted to add a screw thread to easily access the electronics, which ate up several millimeters of margin. But in the end, after several attempts and many hours of work, I managed to finish a decent model in Blender with all the features required by the organization and my teammates.
cansatProject.mod_p3: We then 3D printed the model and saw that everything fit perfectly and that the screw thread worked.
cansatProject.para_p1: We didn't work much on the parachute because we assigned that task to a team member who wasn't doing much, and even so the only task we gave him was never done. It was the main reason we couldn't finish the project, but we do have a photo of a parachute prototype that worked more or less.
cansatProject.doc_p1: This is a report I wrote for my teacher, explaining what we did in the project and reflecting on the work. The document is in Catalan and does not have a translation.
cansatProject.doc_p3: Open it in a new tab

juiceGameJamProject.intro_p1: In early 2025, the Hack Club Slack buzzed about one of the biggest projects to date: a Game Jam where reaching 100 hours of work earned you funding for a trip to China.
juiceGameJamProject.intro_p2: I'm interested in game development, and I've always loved Asian culture — visiting China has been one of my lifelong dreams, so this felt like the best thing that could happen to me.
juiceGameJamProject.idea_p1: My goal was to make a multiplayer shooter in Godot — a big mistake, since half my hours ended up going into fixing bugs caused by player connections. The idea was a kind of 2D, top-down Counter-Strike deathmatch.
juiceGameJamProject.idea_p2: I have a video from the earliest stages of the project showing two players connecting, moving their weapon, and how everything syncs between them.
juiceGameJamProject.fail_p1: The main reason the game was never finished is that I tried to build a multiplayer game without any experience, and because of the deadline I had to patch the code in some pretty hacky ways. Every time I updated something, the multiplayer would break and I'd have to spend an entire evening fixing it — made worse by the fact that Godot's multiplayer was still fairly new, so documentation was scarce.
juiceGameJamProject.trip_p1: Even though my game was unfinished, I reached the 100-hour goal the organizers asked for, so I got to fulfill my dream of going to China. It wasn't easy — the trip was long, tiring, and full of layovers. But in the end, after all those challenges, I had one of the best weeks of my life, meeting incredible people and having a great time. Below is a collection of photos from the trip.

homelabProject.intro: At the High Seas hackathon I was given a 4GB Raspberry Pi. It sat unused for a while because I wasn't sure what to do with it, but one day I decided to build my own humble homelab to solve some problems I had and run services I needed.
homelabProject.domain_p1: My server is accessible from the internet using a domain acquired through Name.com thanks to the GitHub Education program.
homelabProject.domain_p2: To avoid paying for a static IP, I set up a DDNS (Dynamic Domain Name Server). I transferred the domain to Cloudflare since Name.com made it too complicated, and using a script developed by Timothy Miller on GitHub I made the Raspberry Pi check its public IP every few minutes and update the DNS records automatically.
homelabProject.proxy_p1: Each web application on my server runs on a different port to avoid conflicts. To make them all accessible from the internet I set up an Nginx reverse proxy via Docker. Through this container I can route traffic to any service regardless of port, and each one gets its own subdomain.
homelabProject.adguard_p1: On my private network I run my own DNS server that filters requests to block ads, trackers and phishing pages. I can also monitor the network to detect any intruders or unwanted activity.
homelabProject.adguard_p2: I ran into a problem with my router since it didn't allow me to change the DNS in the DHCP settings. I disabled its DHCP and enabled the one built into AdGuard so that every device on my network is protected.
homelabProject.books_p1: I enjoy reading and I'm currently learning Japanese. One of the methods I use is reading, so I set up a server to store my books and read from anywhere without having to download them to my phone or iPad. I use Booklore and access my library from anywhere via the OIDC protocol.
homelabProject.music_p1: This is by far the service I use the most — every single day. I realised streaming subscriptions were expensive and FLAC files offered better quality than Spotify, so I set up my own music server with Navidrome. The only downside is losing the recommendation algorithm that helps discover new music, but it's not a big enough deal to go back to a streaming service.
homelabProject.vpn_p1: To access my local network from an external connection I set up a VPN using WireGuard. As a bonus, I can have AdGuard blocking ads no matter where in the world I am.
